title: The hedge ratio is delta
objectives: Compute delta from a one-step tree and hedge with it.
Show that a delta hedge has zero net payoff in both states, interest included.

screens.title: Selling a call safely
screens.prose: A market maker sells the £100 call for £11.90. If the share rises to £120 she owes £20. She wants no risk in either state.

state.caption: What she owes on the call in a year

screens.question: How many shares should she hold for each call she sold?

options.why: One share per call overshoots: the share moves £40 between the states, the call only £20.
That is $q$, a pricing weight. The hedge matches gains: £20 on the call over £40 on the share.
The £11.90 grows to £12.50 at 5%, short of the £20 she may owe.

hints.text: How much does the call move between the two states? How much does one share move?
The call moves £20 while the share moves £40.
She needs shares that gain £20 when the share gains £40.

feedback.correct: Half a share moves £20, as the call does.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the call’s move between the states.

byKey.one: One share per call overshoots: the share moves £40 between the states, the call only £20.
byKey.none: The £11.90 grows to £12.50 at 5%, short of the £20 she may owe.

explain.text: The call moves £20 when the share moves £40, so half a share moves with it. Holding 0.5 shares per call cancels the call’s risk. This number is the **hedge ratio**, written $\Delta$ and called **delta**.

screens.title: Delta and the strike
screens.prose: Keep the tree at £120 or £80 and change the call’s strike. Watch the payoffs and the hedge ratio move.
screens.question: Which strike gives $\Delta = 0.25$?

hints.text: Slide the strike until the point sits at 0.25.
$\Delta = 0.25$ needs the call to pay a quarter of £40 more when up.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the strike where the point reads 0.25.

byKey.mirror: At £90 the call pays £30 or £0, so $\Delta = 0.75$. Raise the strike.
byKey.quarter: That is a quarter of £100. You need a strike where the call pays £10 if up.

explain.text: At $K = 110$ the call pays £10 or £0, so $\Delta = 10/40 = 0.25$. Below £80 the call pays in both states and $\Delta = 1$. Above £120 it never pays and $\Delta = 0$.

screens.title: The formula you used
screens.prose: Each time you divided the option’s spread by the share’s spread: $$\Delta = \frac{c_u - c_d}{S_u - S_d}.$$ Now take a call struck at £90.
screens.question: What is $\Delta$ for the £90 call?

hints.text: Find the call’s payoff in each state first.
The call pays £30 if up and £0 if down.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the call’s spread by the share’s spread.

byKey.spread: That is the call’s spread in pounds. Divide it by the share’s spread, £40.
byKey.mirror: 0.25 belongs to the £110 call. At £90 the call pays £30 when up.
byKey.one: $\Delta = 1$ needs the call to pay in both states. At £80 the £90 call pays nothing.

explain.text: The call pays £30 or £0, so $\Delta = 30/40 = 0.75$. A lower strike means a bigger up payoff and a bigger delta. The hedge holds 0.75 shares per call sold.

screens.title: The hedged book
screens.prose: Back to the £100 call. She sold it for £11.90, bought 0.5 shares for £50 and borrowed the £38.10 she was short, at 5%. Fill in each line in a year.

state.caption: What she owes on the call

screens.question: Complete the up and down columns.

hints.text: Half a share is worth half the share price. The loan grows by 5% and is owed.
The loan: $38.10 \times 1.05 = 40$, written $-40$.

feedback.correct: Net zero in both states, interest included.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Owing is negative, and the net adds each column.

byKey.r1c2: Half a share at £120 is worth £60.
byKey.r1c3: Half a share at £80 is worth £40.
byKey.r2c2: The loan grows by 5%: $38.10 \times 1.05 = 40$, owed, so $-40$.
byKey.r2c3: She owes the same £40 in the down state.

explain.text: Net zero in both states, after paying the interest. She took no risk and spent nothing. A sold call plus $\Delta$ shares bought with borrowed money is a **delta hedge**.

screens.title: One share per call
screens.prose: A new trader hedges the same sold call with one whole share. He borrows £88.10, the £100 cost less the £11.90 premium, at 5%.
screens.question: What is his net payoff if the share falls?

hints.text: Add the down column.
The loan grows: $88.10 \times 1.05 = 92.50$.

feedback.correct: He loses £12.50 if the share falls, after making £7.50 if it rises.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the down column, interest included.

byKey.hedged: You assumed one share per call is a hedge. The share moves £40 between states and the call only £20, so he is over-hedged.
byKey.no-interest: You repaid £88.10 without interest. At 5% he owes $88.10 \times 1.05 = 92.50$.
byKey.sign: He holds £80 and owes £92.50, so he is down.

explain.text: He makes £7.50 if up and loses £12.50 if down. One share per call carries twice the share risk the call has. Only $\Delta = 0.5$ makes both states zero.

screens.title: A put’s delta
screens.prose: A put struck at £100 pays £0 if the share ends at £120 and £20 if it ends at £80.

state.caption: The put on the same tree

screens.question: What is the put’s $\Delta$?

hints.text: Up minus down, for the put and for the share.
The put’s up payoff is smaller than its down payoff.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take up minus down on top and bottom.

byKey.sign: You took the spread the wrong way round. Up minus down: $(0 - 20)/(120 - 80)$, which is negative.
byKey.spread: That is the put’s spread in pounds. Divide by the share’s spread, £40.

explain.text: $\Delta = (0 - 20)/(120 - 80) = -0.5$. A put loses value as the share rises, so its delta is negative. Its copy sells half a share, as in lesson 2.

screens.title: Deep in, far out
screens.prose: Two more calls on the same tree: one struck at £70, deep in the money, and one at £130, far out of it.
screens.question: What is $\Delta$ for the £70 call?

hints.text: The £70 call pays in both states.
Down, the share at £80 is worth £10 more than the strike.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use both payoffs: £50 and £10.

byKey.up-only: You used £50 over £40 and forgot the £10 it pays if down. The spread is $50 - 10 = 40$.
byKey.half: 0.5 is the £100 call. The £70 call moves £40, pound for pound with the share.

explain.text: The £70 call pays £50 or £10, so $\Delta = 40/40 = 1$: it is sure to be exercised and moves with the share. The £130 call pays nothing in either state, so its $\Delta$ is 0. Delta always lies between 0 and 1 for a call.

screens.title: Delta is a slope
screens.prose: On the chart, $\Delta = \frac{c_u - c_d}{S_u - S_d}$ is the slope of the chord joining the two states. As steps shrink it becomes the slope of the option’s value against the share, $\frac{\partial c}{\partial S}$: the derivative of the limits course, and the partial derivative of multivar.
screens.question: What does the hedge have to match?

options.text: The option’s change between the two states
The payoff’s slope at £120, which is 1
options.why: You took the slope of the payoff right of the strike. The hedge only matches the two states, so it uses the chord.
No chance enters: the chord joins the two possible outcomes, whatever their chances.

options.text: The call’s price over the share’s, $11.90/100$
options.why: That ratio is about 0.12. The hedge depends on how much the option moves, not on what it costs.

hints.text: On the hedged book, what had to be zero?
The net in each state. So the shares must move as much as the option between the two states.

feedback.correct: Delta matches the option’s move between the states.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what the hedged book had to make zero.

explain.text: The hedge must cancel the option in both states, so it matches the rise from $(80, 0)$ to $(120, 20)$. That rise over the run is the chord’s slope, 0.5. With many small steps the chord shrinks to a tangent: that is delta in Black-Scholes.

screens.title: A thousand calls
screens.prose: A market maker sells 1,000 of the £100 calls at the fair price, £11.904762 each before rounding. She delta-hedges the whole book.

state.caption: What the book owes in a year

screens.question: Fill in the hedge. Type numbers without commas.

hints.text: Each call needs $\Delta = 0.5$ shares.
500 shares cost $500 \times 100 = \text{£}50{,}000$.
Premium: $1000 \times 11.904762$. Borrow the rest of the £50,000.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale one call’s hedge by 1,000.

byKey.r0c1: One share per call over-hedges. She needs $1000 \times 0.5$.
byKey.r2c1: She borrows what the premium does not cover: $50{,}000 - 11{,}904.76$, which is $1000 \times 40/1.05$.

explain.text: She holds $1000 \times 0.5 = 500$ shares for £50,000. The premium pays £11,904.76 and she borrows £38,095.24, which grows to £40,000. Rounding each call to £38.10 first would give £38,100: round at the end.

screens.title: Re-hedging
screens.prose: Suppose the share jumps to £110 at once, and from there the tree is £132 or £88. The 1,000 calls are still struck at £100.
screens.question: What is the new $\Delta$ per call?

hints.text: Work out the call’s payoffs on the new tree.
The call pays £32 or £0; the share’s spread is £44.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recompute both spreads on the new tree.

byKey.old: That was delta at £100. The share moved, so the payoffs and the delta moved too.
byKey.spread: That is the call’s spread in pounds. Divide by the share’s, £44.

explain.text: $\Delta = 32/44 = 0.727$, so the book needs about 727 shares, not 500. She buys about 227 more. Delta changes as the share moves, so a hedge must be redone: that is delta hedging, in level 3.

ideas: Delta is the option’s spread over the share’s spread: $\Delta = \frac{c_u - c_d}{S_u - S_d}$.
A sold option plus $\Delta$ shares, financed at the risk-free rate, pays zero in both states.
A call’s delta lies between 0 and 1; a put’s between $-1$ and 0. It changes when the share moves.

formula.name: Hedge ratio
formula.note: The slope of the chord between the two states; in the limit, $\partial c / \partial S$.

summary.trap: One share per option is not a hedge, and a put needs a short position, not a long one.

quiz.prose: The share is at £100 and ends at £120 or £80. A call is struck at £105.
quiz.question: What is the call’s $\Delta$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the call’s spread by the share’s.

byKey.spread: That is the call’s spread in pounds. Divide by £40.
byKey.atm: 0.5 belongs to the £100 call. The £105 call pays only £15 if up.

quiz.prose: Same tree. A put is struck at £110, so it pays £0 if up and £30 if down.
quiz.question: What is the put’s $\Delta$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Up minus down, on top and bottom.

byKey.sign: You dropped the sign. The put pays less when up, so its delta is negative.
byKey.atm: $-0.5$ belongs to the £100 put. This one pays £30 if down.

explain.text: $\Delta = (0 - 30)/(120 - 80) = -0.75$. A higher strike makes the put more sensitive to the share.

quiz.prose: A dealer sells 200 of the £100 puts, each with $\Delta = -0.5$. She wants no risk in either state.
quiz.question: What should she do with the share?

options.why: You copied the put’s sign onto the hedge. A sold put loses when the share falls, so the hedge must gain then: short shares.
That is one share per put. Each put needs only half a share.
If the share falls she owes £20 on each put, £4,000 in all, far above the premiums.

feedback.correct: A sold put has delta $+0.5$; 200 of them need 100 shares short.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out which way the sold puts make her lose.

explain.text: Each sold put has delta $+0.5$, so the book gains £100 per £1 rise in the share. Selling 100 shares short cancels that. She lends the proceeds plus the premiums.

quiz.prose: Same tree. A call is struck at £60.
quiz.question: What is its $\Delta$?

options.why: You divided the up payoff, £60, by £40. It also pays £20 if down, so the spread is £40.
0.5 belongs to the £100 call. This one pays in both states.
Zero belongs to calls that never pay. This one always pays.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find both payoffs first.

explain.text: The £60 call pays £60 or £20: $\Delta = 40/40 = 1$. A call that is sure to be exercised moves pound for pound with the share.
